claims.text: Elevated-temperature degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed primarily by formation and subsequent instability of a protective oxide scale.
The protective scale consists mainly of Al2O3 and Cr2O3.
Synergistic effects between Al and Cr promote rapid oxide formation.
Additive manufacturing produces subtle local elemental segregation in this alloy.
Local elemental segregation creates oxide regions with inferior adhesion and continuity.
Residual stresses from additive manufacturing cause spatially variable oxide adhesion.
Oxidizing exposure produces a locally nonuniform mixed oxide scale.
Composition variations and residual thermal stresses induce scale spallation or discontinuities.
Scale spallation or discontinuities expose the substrate and cause further oxidation.
Reducing H2-containing environments suppress protective oxide formation.
Suppression of oxide formation under reducing conditions promotes matrix elemental depletion and diffusion.
Oxidizing exposure will produce patchy oxide coverage, spallation, and greater surface roughness than the as-manufactured baseline.
Reducing exposure will produce a thinner or absent protective oxide and greater substrate elemental loss.
The as-manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a uniform FCC matrix.
Rapid solidification gives the as-manufactured alloy a relatively homogeneous elemental distribution.
The proposed mechanism applies above approximately 800 °C in strongly oxidizing or strongly reducing environments.
At lower temperatures or under milder atmospheres, oxide-growth and diffusion rates are sufficiently reduced that the proposed mechanism may not apply.

contradictions.description: The initial state and baseline are described as having a uniform or homogeneous elemental distribution, while the central mechanism requires AM-inherent local elemental segregation in that same starting state. Subtle segregation could coexist with macroscopic homogeneity, but the fields do not state that distinction.
